profiles.meeting_scenario: A weekly coordination meeting at a tertiary vascular medicine center that is launching a structured multidisciplinary pathway for newly referred fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) patients. The immediate focus is the next month's first coordinated evaluation day for a small cohort of suspected or confirmed FMD patients, including sequencing imaging, specialist consults, patient education, and documentation handoffs across vascular medicine, radiology, neurology, genetics, and nursing coordination. The agenda is to align on what should happen before the visit, what counts as the standard FMD imaging set, how the shared care plan will be documented, and when patients are considered ready for downstream specialty scheduling. The expected outcome is a shared operational plan for referral triage, visit-day flow, and post-visit handoffs without revisiting major clinical strategy.

members.name: Dr. Elena Marquez
members.role: Vascular Medicine Attending and FMD Program Lead
members.expertise: Vascular medicine, renovascular hypertension, cerebrovascular manifestations of FMD, multidisciplinary clinic design
members.background: An attending physician who trained at a large academic vascular center and is building a formal FMD pathway using registry-informed practice patterns and standardized specialist input.
members.private_state: She wants the new pathway to feel clinically rigorous and consistent with high-volume FMD centers, while keeping physician time protected and avoiding repeated re-review of incomplete referrals.
hidden_assumptions: A 'complete FMD workup' for a new patient generally means one-time cross-sectional head-to-pelvis arterial imaging unless the outside imaging is both recent and already covers that distribution adequately.
When the team says the 'care plan' is ready, it means the physician-authored assessment and follow-up recommendations are finalized in the note and visible to downstream specialists.
If a patient is marked 'ready for scheduling,' the minimum referral package already includes outside image files imported into PACS, not just reports.
The 'first visit' in the coordinated model refers to the on-site multidisciplinary evaluation day after pre-visit chart and imaging review have already occurred.

members.name: Sarah Kim
members.role: Clinical Nurse Coordinator for Vascular Care
members.expertise: Specialty clinic operations, referral intake, patient education, multi-service scheduling, care navigation
members.background: A senior nurse coordinator who previously built streamlined intake workflows in cardiology and now supports the new vascular multidisciplinary clinic with an emphasis on patient throughput and reducing unnecessary repeat testing.
members.private_state: She wants the launch to run smoothly from an operational standpoint, minimize patient travel burden, and avoid holding referrals too long while waiting for perfect records.
hidden_assumptions: A 'complete FMD workup' for scheduling purposes means the core clinically indicated studies for that individual patient are lined up, often using existing outside imaging and filling only obvious gaps rather than defaulting to universal head-to-pelvis imaging.

When the team says the 'care plan' is ready, it means the patient-facing itinerary, education materials, and next-step checklist in the coordinator tracker are assembled well enough to guide the visit.

If a patient is marked 'ready for scheduling,' reports and referral notes are sufficient to reserve coordinated slots, while image transfer can be finished afterward before the actual appointment date.
The 'first visit' in the coordinated model includes the initial intake call and referral review period, because that is when patient expectations, records requests, and education begin.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to getting a 'complete FMD workup' in place before or at the coordinated visit.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a standardized, near-comprehensive vascular evaluation for new FMD patients, typically including head-to-pelvis cross-sectional imaging unless recent outside studies already satisfy that scope.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a pragmatically complete, patient-specific workup sufficient to move the case forward, often relying on available outside studies and ordering only missing pieces.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both interpretations sound clinically responsible and patient-centered, so the phrase signals competence rather than ambiguity; each assumes the other shares the same common-sense clinic definition.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as being 'ready for scheduling'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss referrals being 'ready for scheduling' for the multidisciplinary FMD day.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes a referral is ready only when outside imaging has been imported and reviewed in PACS, making the case mature enough to assign the right specialist sequence and avoid duplicate imaging.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes a referral is ready once the report set, referral note, and provisional visit needs are clear enough to reserve slots, with image transfer still allowed to happen afterward.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In clinic operations, 'ready' often functions as a status shorthand rather than a formal threshold, so both can use the same phrase naturally without noticing they apply different completion criteria.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'care plan' artifact owns the handoff
misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to updating and sharing 'the care plan' after the coordinated visit.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the physician note in the electronic medical record that consolidates diagnostic impression, imaging interpretation, antiplatelet/blood pressure recommendations, and follow-up ownership.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the coordinator's shared tracking document and patient-facing after-visit checklist that lists appointments, pending studies, education items, and phone follow-up tasks.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both artifacts legitimately function as a care plan in multidisciplinary practice, and because each interacts mainly with their own version, the phrase feels mutually obvious instead of requiring disambiguation.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss what should be finished 'before the first visit' versus handled during it.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 treats the first visit as the in-person multidisciplinary evaluation day, so pre-review, records consolidation, and preliminary imaging assessment should occur beforehand.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 treats the first visit as beginning with intake outreach and referral onboarding, so some education, records gathering, and clarification tasks are naturally part of that first-visit process.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are speaking within normal clinic workflow language where 'visit' can mean either the patient-facing appointment day or the broader episode of intake; the overlap in timeline makes the boundary difference easy to miss.

turns.inner_thought: I need this first launch to look like a real FMD program, not an ad hoc consult day. The pathway has to be consistent, clinically defensible, and not create extra physician work because we keep revisiting partial referrals. If we set the expectations now, we can avoid chaos later.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. For next month, I want us to make sure the new FMD referrals move through one consistent multidisciplinary pathway, with as little back-and-forth as possible once they enter the system.

turns.inner_thought: Operationally we're in decent shape if we don't wait for every last piece before moving. A few of these referrals already have enough reports and the referral narrative to start reserving the coordinated day. If I hold them until every image is imported, we'll lose momentum and patients will sit too long.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. On intake, we have a small initial pool that looks appropriate for the first coordinated day, and several of them should be ready for scheduling once the remaining records from this week come in.

turns.inner_thought: Before the in-person multidisciplinary day, I want chart review done, outside imaging in hand, and enough assembled to know whether we truly have the standard head-to-pelvis evaluation covered or what needs to be added. The clinic day should not be when we're first discovering major gaps.
turns.utterance: Good. Before the first visit, I want each new patient to have enough material assembled that we can put a complete FMD workup in place and sequence the specialists thoughtfully.

turns.inner_thought: That's workable if we stay practical. For most of these patients, I can build what I consider a complete FMD workup from the outside CTA, duplex, and referral notes, then just line up whatever obvious missing pieces remain instead of rebuilding everything from scratch.
turns.utterance: I agree. For most of them, I can usually build the complete FMD workup off the outside CTA or duplex reports and then fill in whatever is still missing.

turns.inner_thought: Once a case is actually mature enough for scheduling, I want the images already imported and reviewed so we can tell whether the day should lean neurologic, renal, or more broadly vascular. Otherwise we'll waste specialist slots and end up reacting in real time.
turns.utterance: And once cases are ready for scheduling, I'd like the image review happening early enough that we can decide whether neurology or nephrology needs to be prioritized on the clinic day.

turns.inner_thought: I can absolutely protect the slots once a referral is ready by my intake standards, then keep pushing image transfer in parallel. If I wait to reserve the day until every image is loaded, these patients may miss the launch window.
turns.utterance: Yes, I can do that. As soon as the referrals are ready for scheduling, I can hold the coordinated slots and keep chasing the image transfer before the appointment date.

turns.inner_thought: The handoff has to live in the physician note the same day. PCPs and outside specialists need one authoritative assessment with follow-up ownership, medication decisions, blood pressure management, and surveillance laid out clearly. If that lags, the whole multidisciplinary model looks fuzzy.
turns.utterance: On the back end, I also want the care plan to go out the same day so the PCP and any outside cardiology team know who is following blood pressure, imaging surveillance, and medications.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I can update the shared tracker and patient checklist that afternoon, list pending studies, education points, and next follow-ups, and get everyone moving. That's the practical care plan people actually use after these visits.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. I can update the care plan that same afternoon with the pending studies, education points, and the specialist follow-up checklist for the patient.

turns.inner_thought: I also need radiology and genetics prepared before the on-site day, especially for odd arterial beds or family history questions. They should have enough context from the assembled record and imaging review beforehand, not be seeing the pattern for the first time in clinic.
turns.utterance: One other thing: before the first visit, I'd like genetics and radiology to have enough context to review any unusual vascular distributions rather than discovering them on the clinic day itself.

turns.inner_thought: That's easy to fold into my intake workflow. In my view, the first visit starts when I call the patient and begin onboarding, so I can gather family history, prior vascular events, and outside testing details then. That should give the rest of the team a cleaner starting point.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I'll incorporate those questions into my first-visit intake calls so the team is starting with a cleaner picture.

turns.inner_thought: This all sounds aligned. If we standardize around a full new-patient evaluation, mature referrals before scheduling, and same-day physician documentation, we can launch without constant clarification loops. I just want the workflow to be disciplined from day one.
turns.utterance: Great. So for the launch, we'll use a standard workflow around the complete workup, same-day care plan completion, and smooth scheduling for the coordinated FMD day.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we're aligned enough to move. I'll build this into the referral tracker, start scheduling the current cohort once the remaining records land, and make sure the patient-facing steps and downstream follow-up tasks are all organized under that model.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll operationalize that in the referral tracker and start moving the current referrals through under the shared model.
